messages.claude:
[MPS] Fix torch.clamp to propagate NaN values instead of replacing them (#120899)

Fixes #120899

The previous MPS clamp implementation used `clampWithTensor` (or
`minimumWithPrimaryTensor`/`maximumWithPrimaryTensor` for the single-bound
case), which does not propagate NaN through the operation. As a result,
`torch.clamp` on MPS silently overwrote NaN entries with the supplied
min/max bound — e.g. `torch.clamp(t, min=-100, max=100)` returned `-100`
for NaN positions — while CPU and CUDA preserve NaN, leading to divergent
results across backends.

To match the CPU/CUDA contract that NaN inputs remain NaN, replace the
single `clampWithTensor` call with a composition of
`minimumWithNaNPropagationWithPrimaryTensor` and
`maximumWithNaNPropagationWithPrimaryTensor`, applied in sequence over the
(input, max) and (input, min) pairs respectively. The min-only / max-only
cases now also use the NaN-propagating variants so that all three forms
(min&max, min-only, max-only) behave consistently with respect to NaN.

Add `test_clamp_nan` covering min&max, min-only, and max-only paths to
guard against regressions on the MPS backend.

messages.claude:
[MPS] Fix fill_scalar regression on macOS 14.4+ by using scalar placeholder feed (#122016)

Replaces the `constantWithScalar` op in `fill_scalar_mps_impl` with a
scalar placeholder tensor that is fed at run time. The previous
implementation baked the scalar value into the graph as a constant,
which produced garbage/incorrect values for `torch.fill_scalar` (and
callers like `rms_norm` on the `transformers` path) starting on macOS
14.4. The regression was tracked down to the constant-baking commit
056d6247 and reported in #122016.

What:
- Add an `inputTensor_` placeholder to the CachedGraph and create it via
  `mpsGraphScalarPlaceHolder` instead of `constantWithScalar`.
- Build a `feeds` dictionary from `getMPSScalar`/`getMPSGraphTensorFromScalar`
  on the current MPS stream and pass it to `runMPSGraph` (previously
  `nil`).
- Drop the bool/uint8 cast workarounds that existed only to paper over
  `constantWithScalar` quirks (issues #82427, #83692); with a fed
  placeholder the value is materialized in the correct dtype directly.
- Enable `nn.functional.rms_norm` in the MPS op tests so the path that
  originally surfaced the regression is covered.

Why:
`constantWithScalar` constructs the tensor at graph-build time and, on
macOS 14.4+, returns wrong results for certain dtypes/shapes. By feeding
the scalar as runtime tensor data the value is no longer captured in the
cached graph, sidestepping the broken constant path and ensuring
`fill_scalar` produces correct values across macOS versions. This also
unblocks downstream users (e.g. `transformers` beam search / `rms_norm`)
that hit the bad values on startup.

Fixes #122016

The problematic commit (056d6247c786f4391bc6a6f21337b009c7e9699e) used `constantWithScalar` which appears to have issues on macOS 14.4. The fix uses a placeholder approach to work around this.

test: refactor and split test_open_device_registration to fix flaky CI

Split the monolithic `test_open_device_registration` into independent test
cases (test_base_device_registration, test_common_registration,
test_open_device_generator_registration_and_hooks, test_open_device_dispatchstub,

- Issue #100152 reports `test_open_device_registration` as flaky/disabled in

messages.claude:
fix: handle checkpoint prefix removal in _get_fqns for FSDP optimizer state loading

When loading optimizer state separately from a checkpoint with FSDP (use_orig_params=False + activation checkpointing), _get_fqns would fail because the checkpoint prefix was only stripped from the short-circuit return path. Once the function proceeded past the single-segment branch, the prefix remained in the FQN and broke downstream lookups (issue #124546).

Move the _CHECKPOINT_PREFIX.replace() to the top of the function so the prefix is removed consistently for all code paths, including the FSDP flat_param branch. The old comment claiming "FSDP already handles removal of checkpoint prefix" is removed since the prefix is now stripped before reaching that branch.
messages.kimi:
fix: Handle checkpoint prefix removal in FQNs for FSDP with activation checkpointing

Summary:
Fix FQN resolution in distributed checkpointing when using FSDP with `use_orig_params=False` and activation checkpointing. The checkpoint prefix was not being properly stripped before processing FQNs, causing KeyError when loading optimizer state separately from the checkpoint.

The change moves the checkpoint prefix removal to the beginning of `_get_fqns()` function, ensuring the prefix is stripped before any FQN processing occurs. This prevents incorrect FQN matching when FSDP's flat parameter handling is involved.

Why:
When loading optimizer state through `torch.distributed.checkpoint.load()`, the FQN resolution fails because the checkpoint prefix (added by activation checkpointing) interferes with FSDP's internal FQN mapping. The previous code only removed the prefix in the simple case (no dots in name), but not before the FSDP flat parameter processing path, leading to mismatched FQNs and failed state dict loading.

Issue: #124546
messages.minimax:
fix: correct FQN computation when loading optimizer state with FSDP

When using distributed checkpointing with FSDP, `use_orig_params=False`, and activation checkpointing, loading the optimizer state threw errors due to malformed FQNs.

The root cause was inconsistent handling of the checkpoint prefix in `_get_fqns`: when the name contained no ".", the prefix was removed in the return statement, but in the FSDPwrapped module branch the prefix removal was delegated to FSDP itself with an assumption that it would be handled. This caused FQN mismatches during optimizer state loading.

The fix removes the checkpoint prefix once upfront before any further processing, ensuring consistent FQN computation regardless of the code path taken.

Issue #122792: [DCP] `set_model_state_dict` errors on compiled module with non-persistent buffer
```
"""
torchrun --standalone --nproc_per_node=2 repro_dcp_compile.py
"""
import os
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.distributed as dist
from torch.distributed.checkpoint.state_dict import get_model_state_dict, set_model_state_dict

class Model(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.lin1 = nn.Linear(4, 4)
        self.lin2 = nn.Linear(4, 4)
        self.register_buffer("buf", torch.randn((4,)), persistent=False)
        self.weight = nn.Parameter(torch.randn((4, 4)))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    dist.init_process_group(backend="nccl")
    gpu_id = int(os.environ["LOCAL_RANK"])
    device = f"cuda:{gpu_id}"
    torch.cuda.set_device(device)

    model = Model()
    model = torch.compile(model)

    sharded_sd = get_model_state_dict(model)
    set_model_state_dict(model, sharded_sd)
```

```
[rank0]: Traceback (most recent call last):
[rank0]:   File "/data/users/andgu/pytorch/repro_dcp_compile.py", line 36, in <module>
[rank0]:     set_model_state_dict(model, sharded_sd)
[rank0]:   File "/data/users/andgu/pytorch/torch/distributed/checkpoint/state_dict.py", line 853, in set_model_state_dict
[rank0]:     return _load_model_state_dict(model, model_state_dict, info)
[rank0]:   File "/data/users/andgu/pytorch/torch/distributed/checkpoint/state_dict.py", line 416, in _load_model_state_dict
[rank0]:     state_dict[fqn_with_prefix] = state_dict.pop(fqn)
[rank0]: KeyError: 'buf'
```

`set_model_state_dict` calls into `_load_model_state_dict`, which iterates over `named_buffers()`. For a compiled module, `fqns` and `fqns_with_prefix` always mismatch, so `_load_model_state_dict` will try to reassign from the FQN without prefix to the one with prefix. However, this does not account for non-persistent buffers not existing in the state dict.

One solution could be just to continue `if fqn not in state_dict`.



cc @LucasLLC

fix: skip non-persistent buffers in DCP state_dict traversal

When iterating over a module's buffers in `recurse`, `_non_persistent_buffers_set` was not consulted, so non-persistent buffers were yielded as load targets. For compiled modules, `_load_model_state_dict` then tries to remap `buf` to its prefixed FQN and fails with `KeyError: 'buf'` because non-persistent buffers never appear in the state dict.

Fixes #122792

Pull Request resolved: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/122793
messages.kimi:
fix: Skip non-persistent buffers in DCP state dict operations

The `get_model_state_dict` function was incorrectly including non-persistent buffers in the returned state dict, causing `set_model_state_dict` to fail with a KeyError when trying to load the state back. This occurred because the recursive FQN generation logic iterated over all buffers without checking if they were marked as non-persistent.

By checking `module._non_persistent_buffers_set` and skipping those buffers during FQN generation, we ensure that non-persistent buffers (which are intentionally excluded from `state_dict()`) are also excluded from distributed checkpoint operations. This aligns DCP behavior with PyTorch's standard state dict semantics where `persistent=False` buffers should not be saved or loaded.

Fixes #122792

Triton codegen currently [sorts vars by divisor](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/ae6f6b8efb6380a94621d61100ffb05dab05db27/torch/_inductor/codegen/simd.py#L233-L237). When there are two vars with the same divisor, the order is undecided.

```python
nodes.sort(
   key=lambda x: V.graph.sizevars.size_hint(
       x.divisor, fallback=config.unbacked_symint_fallback
   )
)
```

The test case leads to the following nodes:
```
(Pdb) nodes[0]
IterationRangesEntry(x1, ((s37 + 127)//128), 2, (xindex//ps0), {x0: ((s37 + 127)//128), x1: 2, x2: ((s12 + 127)//128), x4: 2*(((s12 + 127)//128))*(((s37 + 127)//128)), x5: 0, x6: 2, x7: (((s12 + 127)//128))*(((s37 + 127)//128))})

(Pdb) nodes[1]
IterationRangesEntry(x0, 1, ((s37 + 127)//128), ModularIndexing(xindex, 1, ps0), {x0: ((s37 + 127)//128), x1: 2, x2: ((s12 + 127)//128), x4: 2*(((s12 + 127)//128))*(((s37 + 127)//128)), x5: 0, x6: 2, x7: (((s12 + 127)//128))*(((s37 + 127)//128))})

(Pdb) nodes[2]
IterationRangesEntry(x2, 2*(((s37 + 127)//128)), ((s12 + 127)//128), (xindex//(2*(((s37 + 127)//128)))), {x0: ((s37 + 127)//128), x1: 2, x2: ((s12 + 127)//128), x4: 2*(((s12 + 127)//128))*(((s37 + 127)//128)), x5: 0, x6: 2, x7: (((s12 + 127)//128))*(((s37 + 127)//128))})

(Pdb) V.graph.sizevars.statically_known_equals(nodes[0].length, 2)
True
(Pdb) V.graph.sizevars.statically_known_equals(nodes[1].length, 1)
True
(Pdb) V.graph.sizevars.statically_known_equals(nodes[2].length, 1)
True

(Pdb) V.graph.sizevars.statically_known_equals(nodes[0].divisor, 1)
True
(Pdb) V.graph.sizevars.statically_known_equals(nodes[1].divisor, 1)
True
(Pdb) V.graph.sizevars.statically_known_equals(nodes[2].divisor, 2)
True
```

Since x1 and x0 both have divisor 1, the relative order is random across runs.
In some runs, we have order [x1, x0, x2] with divisors as [1,1,2] and lengths as [2,1,1]. After x1, we have [divisor = divisor * node.length](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/ae6f6b8efb6380a94621d61100ffb05dab05db27/torch/_inductor/codegen/simd.py#L246) = 1 * 2 = 2. Then, when processing x0, we have node.divisor=1, divisor=2, and [FloorDiv(node.divisor, divisor)](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/ae6f6b8efb6380a94621d61100ffb05dab05db27/torch/_inductor/codegen/simd.py#L251) = 0, which indicates an iteration length of 0 and leads errors later.

The fix is to sort by both divisor and length_is_one. So for two nodes with the same divisor, we process the node with length=1 first.

Fixes #149789

[Inductor][CPP] Fix Codegen Issue when Parallel Reduction under the vectorization (#151887)

**Summary**
Fixes [#151290](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/151290) and [#151523](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/151523), which are regressions introduced by [#144020](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/144020). That PR enabled parallelization at the inner loop level.

However, a currently unsupported case arises when parallel reduction occurs under the vectorization loop level, specifically in patterns like:
```
for vec_loop_level:
    do_parallel_reduction
```
In such cases, a temporary buffer `tmp_acc_array` is allocated for tail scalar kernels, and another temporary buffer `tmp_acc_array` is also defined for parallel reduction. This results in a conflict due to overlapping temporary buffers. This PR disables the problematic case to avoid the conflict until proper support is implemented.

**Test Plan**
```
python test/inductor/test_flex_attention.py -k test_make_block_mask_cpu
python test/inductor/test_cpu_repro.py -k test_parallel_reduction_vectorization
```

messages.kimi:
1. test/inductor/test_flex_attention.py: Modifies a test to use a fudge factor for memory access metrics, with a TODO comment explaining why (unnecessary materialization and extraneous logsumexp writes)

2. test/inductor/test_mkldnn_pattern_matcher.py: Adds a new `num_include_ops` parameter to verify the exact count of specific operations in generated code, with different assertions for CPP wrapper vs Python wrapper

3. torch/_inductor/ir.py: Changes the `MutationOutput` class to include `node_doing_mutating` in the inputs list and removes the custom `get_read_writes` method that was adding a WeakDep

The core fix is in `ir.py` - it's fixing how mutation dependencies are tracked. The issue #127402 mentions accuracy drops and performance improvements in quantization, which suggests the mutation tracking fix ensures proper dependencies are maintained during code generation.

This is a fix type commit that corrects the dependency tracking in the IR to prevent issues with quantization patterns.

fix: Correct MutationOutput dependency tracking to include node_doing_mutating in inputs

The MutationOutput class was not properly including node_doing_mutating in its inputs list, instead relying on a custom get_read_writes() method to add a WeakDep. This caused incorrect dependency tracking that led to accuracy drops and abnormal performance improvements in quantization patterns, as operations could be incorrectly reordered or eliminated.

By including node_doing_mutating directly in the inputs passed to the parent constructor, we ensure proper dependency tracking through the standard IR dependency mechanism rather than the custom WeakDep workaround. This fixes the quantization accuracy issues reported in #127402 where operations were not being properly sequenced.

The test changes add verification for the correct number of quantized linear operations and adjust memory access assertions to account for the now-correct behavior.
messages.claude:
fix: include mutating node in Mutation dependence via input list rather than WeakDep

The Mutation IR node previously established its dependence on the node performing the mutation by overriding get_read_writes() to inject a dependencies.WeakDep on node_doing_mutating. This workaround caused two problems observed in the inductor:

1. Unnecessary materialization of attention outputs. In test_flex_attention.py the memory-access metric test had to assert exact equality against accessed_bytes * num_accesses + logsumexp_bytes. Because the WeakDep did not create a true data dependency, the mutated output was being materialized unnecessarily (related to how mutation is handled), and an extraneous logsumexp was also written. The test is relaxed to assertLess with a fudge factor and a TODO documenting the remaining materialization, which is the observable symptom of the underlying dependence issue.

2. OneDNN quantization codegen regression (issue #127402). HuggingFace static/dynamic quantization models showed abnormal accuracy drops (e.g. text-classification models dropping from ~0.68 to 0.3162) alongside a misleading speedup on the 2024-05-26 nightly. With cpp_wrapper enabled, the fused op_qlinear_pointwise.call / op_qlinear_pointwise_binary.call calls were not being emitted in the expected counts because the mutation dependence was too weak to keep the producer alive through fusion, collapsing pointwise fusions and degrading accuracy. test_mkldnn_pattern_matcher.py now asserts the exact count of these ops via the new num_include_ops parameter for both cpp and python wrappers.

The fix replaces the WeakDep injection by passing node_doing_mutating directly as an input to the Mutation node (super().__init__(None, layout, [mutated_node, node_doing_mutating], ())), and removes the get_read_writes() override. This makes the mutation dependence a real data edge in the graph, so downstream fusion/codegen treats the mutating node as a genuine consumer of the buffer, fixing both the materialization and the quantization codegen regressions.

Fixes #127402

Issue #128444: HSDP + `set_optimizer_state_dict` errors with monolithic checkpointing
### 🐛 Describe the bug

PyTorch 2.3.1 (and nightly)

### Versions

TLDR: HSDP + DCP monolith checkpointing break.

When using DCP + `set_optimizer_state_dict`, the code eventually goes to `_optim_state_dict_to_load_impl` [here](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/adb699189b9d2de7cfbd71e59c70d916483b23dd/torch/distributed/fsdp/fully_sharded_data_parallel.py#L1298), which calls `_flatten_optim_state_dict` and in turn `_broadcast_processed_state` defined [here](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/adb699189b9d2de7cfbd71e59c70d916483b23dd/torch/distributed/fsdp/_optim_utils.py#L338). 

```
def _broadcast_processed_state(
    fsdp_state: _FSDPState,
    optim_state: Dict[str, Any],
    group: Optional[dist.ProcessGroup],
) -> Dict[str, Any]:
    objects: List[Any] = [None]
    if fsdp_state.rank == 0:
        objects[0] = tree_map_only(
            torch.Tensor,
            lambda v: v.cpu() if v.dim() == 0 else _PosDimTensorInfo(v.shape, v.dtype),  # type: ignore[union-attr]
            optim_state,
        )
    dist.broadcast_object_list(objects, src=0, group=group)
    if fsdp_state.rank == 0:
        return optim_state
    else:
        return objects[0]
```

This broadcast occurs across the specified group, which is `None` -> global processs group (as `set_optimizer_state_dict` has no way of specifying the group). However, when using HSDP, `fsdp_state.rank` is the local rank within the shard group and not the global rank. Thus, local rank 0 of each shard group will error out as it returns `optim_state`, which is set to `None` in `_optim_state_dict_to_load_impl` [here](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/70a1e8571802c22c0f09279b77876e6e85c81325/torch/distributed/fsdp/fully_sharded_data_parallel.py#L1338-L1339). 

```
        if rank0_only and dist.get_rank(group) > 0:
            optim_state_dict = {}
```

I think the correct solution is to check for rank in the same group as the broadcast but not 100% sure

cc @mrshenli @pritamdamania87 @zhaojuanmao @satgera @gqchen @aazzolini @osalpekar @jiayisuse @H-Huang @kwen2501 @awgu @penguinwu @fegin @XilunWu @wanchaol @fduwjj @wz337 @tianyu-l @wconstab @yf225 @chauhang @d4l3k @LucasLLC @MeetVadakkanchery

messages.kimi:
fix: Use correct rank check in HSDP optimizer state broadcast

Change `fsdp_state.rank` to `dist.get_rank(group)` in `_broadcast_processed_state` and `_broadcast_state` to correctly identify the broadcast source rank within the specified process group. 

When using HSDP (Hybrid Sharded Data Parallel), `fsdp_state.rank` returns the local rank within the shard group, not the global rank. This causes incorrect behavior during optimizer state dict loading with DCP monolithic checkpointing because the broadcast operates on the global process group (or specified group), but the rank check uses the local shard rank. Local rank 0 of each shard group incorrectly returns `optim_state` instead of receiving from the actual global rank 0, leading to errors when `optim_state` is `None` for non-zero global ranks. Using `dist.get_rank(group)` ensures the rank check is consistent with the broadcast group, fixing the HSDP + `set_optimizer_state_dict` compatibility issue.
messages.claude:
fix(fsdp): use group-relative rank in _broadcast_processed_state/_broadcast_state for HSDP

What:
Replace `fsdp_state.rank == 0` checks with `dist.get_rank(group) == 0` in
`_broadcast_processed_state` and `_broadcast_state` in
`torch/distributed/fsdp/_optim_utils.py`, so the rank-0 check uses the
same process group as the subsequent `dist.broadcast_object_list` call.

Why:
With HSDP, `fsdp_state.rank` is the local rank within the shard group,
not the global rank. When `set_optimizer_state_dict` is used with
monolithic/DCP checkpointing, the broadcast group passed in is `None`
(i.e. the global process group, since there is no way to specify a
group), while the rank check was still based on the shard-local rank.
As a result, local rank 0 of every shard group incorrectly treated
itself as the broadcast source: it returned the local `optim_state`
(which `_optim_state_dict_to_load_impl` had already set to `None` for
non-global-rank-0), producing broken/`None` optimizer state on load
(issue #128444). Aligning the rank check with the broadcast group
ensures only global rank 0 acts as the source, matching the broadcast
semantics and fixing the HSDP + `set_optimizer_state_dict` checkpoint
load path.
messages.minimax:
fix [FSDP] Use dist.get_rank(group) instead of fsdp_state.rank in _broadcast_* functions

When using HSDP with set_optimizer_state_dict and monolithic checkpointing (DCP), the broadcast operation used fsdp_state.rank to determine rank 0. However, fsdp_state.rank is the local rank within the shard group, not the global rank within the broadcast group. This caused every local rank 0 in each shard group to incorrectly enter the rank-0 branch, leading to errors since the broadcast's src=0 refers to global rank 0.

The fix replaces fsdp_state.rank == 0 with dist.get_rank(group) == 0 in _broadcast_processed_state and _broadcast_state, ensuring the rank check matches the broadcast's group context.

Fixes #128444

exemplars.message:
Reland fast gather and index implementation (#151917)

This PR reapplies #151490 and #151753 together, and adds some missing checks when applying the fast path.
Previously missed checks:
1) indexing path has the stride in the indexed dimension in bytes, gather path has the stride in the indexed dimension in elements. When checking if fast path is applicable, I didn't take this difference into account, and still multiplied the indexing stride by element size. Fixed and test added
2) We want to take fast path only when we are copying contiguous equally spaced slices of inputs + all the necessary alignment requirements. The effective tensor size should be 2d (after all possible flattening is applied), the index stride in the last dimension should be 0, and, since in the kernel we are not applying non-indexing-related offsets to src tensor, the src tensor stride in the second dimension should be 0. This automatically happens for gather with dim=0, so I didn't put in an explicit condition for this. Sometimes all conditions except first dim "effective" stride equal to 0 are satisfied for scatter on non-zero dim, when index size in the indexing dimension is 1 and thus it is collapsed (dimensions of size 1 are always collapsed), e.g.
```
        # test gather along 1st dim that can accidentally trigger fast path
        # because due to index dimension in the gather dim being 1
        # an unexpected squashing in tensorIterator happens
        src = make_tensor((16, 2, 16), device=device, dtype=dtype)
        ind = torch.randint(2, (16, 1), device=device).view(16, 1, 1).expand(16, 1, 16)
        res = torch.gather(src, dim=1, index=ind)
        if res.device.type == "cuda":
            ref_cpu = torch.gather(src.cpu(), dim=1, index=ind.cpu())
            self.assertEqual(res.cpu(), ref_cpu, atol=0, rtol=0)
```
Note that if index size here was (16, 2, 16) instead of (16, 1, 16) then the middle dimension could not be collapsed and we wouldn't end up incorrectly taking fast path.
We could update the kernel to take this stride into account when computing offsets into src tensor, or we could specifically disallow non-zero stride on the first dimension. I took the second path for now.

Provide access to the cudaGraph_t underlying a CUDAGraph. (#155164)

There are a few considerations here:

1. A user might want to modify the cudaGraph_t either during the stream capture or after the stream capture (but before instantiation). This draft implements modification after stream capture only, though support could be added for modification during stream capture by applying
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/140979/files#diff-d7302d133bb5e0890fc94de9aeea4d9d442555a3b40772c9db10edb5cf36a35cR391-R404

2. Previously, the cudaGraph_t would be destroyed before the end of capture_end() unless the user had previously called enable_debug_mode(). There is no way to implement this correctly without removing this restriction, or forcing the user to always call enable_debug_mode(). However, enable_debug_mode() is a confusing API (despite being an instance method, it would modify a static global variable; thus, putting one CUDAGraph object into debug mode puts all of them into debug mode, which is not acceptable in my opinion). Therefore, I made enable_debug_mode() into a no-op. This means that the CPU memory usage will increase after this change. I think this is likely to be fine.

3. No python bindings yet. These should be easy to add. It is probably worthwhile to take some time to make sure that the returned cudaGraph_t can be converted into the cuda-python cudaGraph_t in a reasonable, hopefully type-safe, manner (but without making cuda-python a dependency of pytorch), since I imagine most users will use the pip cuda-python package to make modifications.

4. There are two foot guns:

   a. The cudaGraph_t returned by raw_cuda_graph() is not owned by the user, so it will be destroyed once the owning CUDAGraph is destroyed (or calls reset()).

   b. The following seuquence won't work as intended:

```
g = torch.cuda.CUDAGraph()
with torch.cuda.graph(g):
    foo()
g.replay()
raw_graph = g.raw_cuda_graph()
modify(raw_graph)
g.replay()
```

This won't work because the user must call instantiate() again after modifying cudaGraph_t. You could add a "safety" mechanism by traversing the cudaGraph_t to create a hash and seeing if the hash changes between calls to replay(), but this is likely way too expensive.

I think these two foot guns are probably okay given that this a bit of an experts' API.

messages.kimi:
fix: Remove incorrect assertion preventing CUDA graph unregistration during cleanup

Remove the `assertNotCapturing` check in `CUDAGeneratorState::unregister_graph()` that was causing crashes when CUDA graphs are destroyed during exception handling or process shutdown.

The assertion was overly restrictive and would trigger when unregistration happens during cleanup phases, such as when handling async CUDA assertions. The check is unnecessary because the actual safety of graph unregistration is guaranteed by other mechanisms in the CUDA graph lifecycle management.

Fixes #125804
messages.claude:
fix: remove capturing-stage assertion in CUDAGeneratorState::unregister_graph

What:
Removed the `at::cuda::assertNotCapturing` check (and its accompanying
comment) at the top of `CUDAGeneratorState::unregister_graph` in
`aten/src/ATen/cuda/CUDAGeneratorImpl.cpp`. The function still verifies
that the graph was previously registered via the existing
`registered_graphs_` lookup.

Why:
Issue #125804 reports a `torch.compile` crash where `_assert_async_cuda_kernel`
fires an assertion (`input[0] != 0`) on a CUDA tensor, and the resulting
exception unwinds through `CUDAGeneratorState::unregister_graph`. The stack
trace terminates in that function, and the process aborts with exit code 134
("Aborted (core dumped)").

The root cause is that when a CUDA graph captured during `torch.compile`
is torn down (e.g. the compiled callable is destroyed or recompiled while
a capture is still in flight), the destructor path calls `unregister_graph`.
The pre-existing `assertNotCapturing` check raises an exception while the
CUDA stream is still in a capturing stage, and raising an exception during
stack unwinding triggers `std::terminate` -> `abort`. This is why the
minirepro from the issue aborts the whole process instead of printing the
"ignoring exception" message and exiting cleanly.

Dropping the assertion allows `unregister_graph` to proceed during tear-down
even when capture is still active, so cleanup no longer turns a recoverable
exception into a fatal abort. The subsequent `TORCH_CHECK` against
`registered_graphs_` still guards the actual state mutation, so unregistered
graphs continue to be rejected.
messages.minimax:
fix: remove overly restrictive assertion in CUDAGeneratorState::unregister_graph

The `assertNotCapturing` check in `CUDAGeneratorState::unregister_graph()` was causing a crash (segfault) when `torch._assert_async` was called within a `torch.compile` context. The assertion prevented graph unregistration during capture stage, but this restriction was too aggressive and led to aborts on process exit when CUDA graphs were involved. Removing this check allows proper cleanup of CUDA graph state in these scenarios.

Fixes #125804

feat: Add support for ncclRemoteError in NCCL result code mapping

Add ncclRemoteError to the ncclResult enum and update the bidirectional conversion functions (to_nccl_result and from_nccl_result) to handle the new error code. This aligns PyTorch's NCCL bindings with NCCL 2.14.3+ which introduced ncclRemoteError for handling remote worker failures.

Fixes #128756
messages.claude:
fix: Add missing ncclRemoteError to ncclResult enum

NCCL 2.14.3 introduced a new ncclRemoteError result code, but PyTorch's ncclResult enum did not include it, causing from_nccl_result to throw std::runtime_error("Unconvertible NCCL type") when a remote NCCL worker fails. This prevented graceful handling of remote failures in distributed training.

Updates torch/csrc/cuda/nccl.h to insert RemoteError=6 and shift NumResults to 8 (matching the upstream NCCL ordering), and adds the corresponding case branches in both to_nccl_result and from_nccl_result so remote errors round-trip correctly.

Fixes #128756

messages.kimi:
fix: Fix DCP in-place loading for optimizer state dict

The `_init_state_dict` function in `planner_helpers.py` was not properly performing in-place initialization of tensors. It was using `tree_map_only` (non-inplace) and then manually reassigning keys, which broke the in-place loading contract that DCP promises. This caused the optimizer learning rate and other non-tensor state to not be properly loaded from checkpoints, resulting in regressions where the initial learning rate was used instead of the checkpointed one.

The fix switches to `tree_map_only_` (the inplace version) which correctly modifies tensors in place, preserving the object identity required for proper state dict loading. A new test `TestInitStateDict` is added to verify that loaded state dicts maintain object identity and that optimizer parameters like learning rate are correctly restored from checkpoints.
messages.claude:
fix: ensure DCP in-place loading restores optimizer non-tensor state like learning rate

Switches `_init_state_dict` to use the in-place `tree_map_only_` instead of
`tree_map_only` + manual reassignment. The previous non-in-place path replaced
state_dict entries with meta tensors in a way that broke in-place loading for
optimizer param_groups, so non-tensor fields such as `lr` were never restored
from the checkpoint — a regression introduced in 2.3.0 (issue #129079), where
the first step after resume used the initialization learning rate rather than
the checkpointed one.

Using `tree_map_only_` preserves the original container identity so DCP's
claimed in-place loading semantics actually hold: optimizer param_groups are
updated in place and `lr` is correctly restored.

Adds `TestInitStateDict.test_init_state_dict` to cover the in-place contract:
it saves a model+optimizer (lr=0.1), loads into a fresh optimizer with lr=0.2,
and asserts the loaded containers are the same objects and that
`optim_2.param_groups[0]["lr"]` is 0.1 after `set_state_dict`.

Fixes #129079.
messages.minimax:
fix: use inplace tree_map_only_ in _init_state_dict to fix optimizer lr regression

The `_init_state_dict` function was using `tree_map_only` which creates a separate dict with meta tensors, then manually assigns each key back to the original state_dict. This approach broke the in-place loading semantics for optimizer state dicts, causing the learning rate to not be restored correctly from checkpoints (issue #129079).

The fix switches to `tree_map_only_` (inplace version) which modifies tensors directly in the state_dict without creating an intermediate dict, preserving the object references needed for correct in-place loading.

[aten] Enable vectorized 8byte copy for fp16/bf16 for index select kernel (#152380) ## Summary Enable aligned vector loading for 2 bytes data types for index select. Specifically: - **4 element fp16/bf16 packing**: added 8-byte vector load/store to move 4 half values at once. - **warp-wide predicate (__all_sync)**: decide fast vs fallback path per warp, eliminating lane level divergence - **alignment guard**: fast or vectorized path only executes when src and dst are 8 byte aligned, preventing mis aligned address faults. - **Safe for loop fallback**: for misaligned, strid > 1, or tail elements we recompute offsets per element to avoid memory corruption. - **Bound checks**: fast or vectorized path is skipped when less than 4 elements are remaining, guaranteeing bounded access. - **Stride remapping**: Redirect calls to inner contiguous dim which has stride = 1 so copies occur along memory coalesced axes. - **AMD support**: Ensured portability and correctness across CUDA and HIP platforms. ## Perf testing We note a 2.5x improvement in memory bandwidth after this change when the tensor dim is a multiple of 4 for 2 byte data types (fp16/bf16). Make torch._chunk_cat support non-contiguous inputs (#151263)

Currently, `torch._chunk_cat` only supports contiguous inputs (due to `.view()` usage in `_pad_chunk()` supporting only contiguous tensor). This doesn't work for internal models where there can be non-contiguous input tensors:

- size=[8192, 16416], stride=[16448, 1]  # stride[0] is larger than size[1]
- size=[1152, 384], stride=[1, 1152]  # column-major tensor

In this PR, we relax the assumption on contiguous input tensor, by switching from `.view()` to `.reshape()`. Note that since `.reshape()` will try to use `.view()` under the hood whenever possible, this should not cause regression to existing use cases.

Approved by: https://github.com/BoyuanFeng

Reland fast gather and index implementation (#151917)

This PR reapplies #151490 and #151753 together, and adds some missing checks when applying the fast path.
Previously missed checks:
1) indexing path has the stride in the indexed dimension in bytes, gather path has the stride in the indexed dimension in elements. When checking if fast path is applicable, I didn't take this difference into account, and still multiplied the indexing stride by element size. Fixed and test added
2) We want to take fast path only when we are copying contiguous equally spaced slices of inputs + all the necessary alignment requirements. The effective tensor size should be 2d (after all possible flattening is applied), the index stride in the last dimension should be 0, and, since in the kernel we are not applying non-indexing-related offsets to src tensor, the src tensor stride in the second dimension should be 0. This automatically happens for gather with dim=0, so I didn't put in an explicit condition for this. Sometimes all conditions except first dim "effective" stride equal to 0 are satisfied for scatter on non-zero dim, when index size in the indexing dimension is 1 and thus it is collapsed (dimensions of size 1 are always collapsed), e.g.
```
        # test gather along 1st dim that can accidentally trigger fast path
        # because due to index dimension in the gather dim being 1
        # an unexpected squashing in tensorIterator happens
        src = make_tensor((16, 2, 16), device=device, dtype=dtype)
        ind = torch.randint(2, (16, 1), device=device).view(16, 1, 1).expand(16, 1, 16)
        res = torch.gather(src, dim=1, index=ind)
        if res.device.type == "cuda":
            ref_cpu = torch.gather(src.cpu(), dim=1, index=ind.cpu())
            self.assertEqual(res.cpu(), ref_cpu, atol=0, rtol=0)
```
Note that if index size here was (16, 2, 16) instead of (16, 1, 16) then the middle dimension could not be collapsed and we wouldn't end up incorrectly taking fast path.
We could update the kernel to take this stride into account when computing offsets into src tensor, or we could specifically disallow non-zero stride on the first dimension. I took the second path for now.

Approved by: https://github.com/eqy, https://github.com/malfet, https://github.com/Skylion007

messages.kimi:
fix: Fix invalid configuration argument error in F.embedding on ROCm with large tensors

Summary

Fixes issue #130806 where `F.embedding` crashes with "invalid configuration argument" error on AMD GPUs when processing large tensors. The root cause was twofold:

1. Signed integer overflow: `ptrdiff_t` (signed) was used for tensor size calculations, causing overflow when `outTotalSize >= 2147483648` (2^31)
2. ROCm `std::min` issue: On ROCm, `std::min` with `::min` did not work correctly when `outTotalSize >= 2147483648`

Changes

- Changed `getSliceSize` return type and local variables from `ptrdiff_t` to `size_t` (unsigned)
- Updated `index_add_cuda_impl`, `index_reduce_func_cuda_impl`, and `index_select_out_cuda_impl` to use `uint64_t` instead of `ptrdiff_t`/`int64_t` for size calculations
- Fixed `largeIndexBlock` calculation to use conditional operator instead of `std::min` to avoid ROCm issue with large values
- Added test case `test_large_tensors` to verify embedding works with tensors containing 2,147,483,648 elements

Pull Request resolved: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/XXXXXX
messages.claude:
fix: resolve large tensor overflow in CUDA index_select/embedding (#130806)

Switch indexing kernel size variables from signed ptrdiff_t/int64_t to
uint64_t across index_add, index_reduce, and index_select CUDA paths.
Previously, slice sizes and total sizes derived from numel() were stored
in signed types, so tensors with outTotalSize >= 2147483648 (2^31)
overflowed the 32-bit signed range used to size the largeIndexBlock
dim3, producing "HIP error: invalid configuration argument" on ROCm
(and silently wrong grid/block configs on CUDA) for F.embedding with
large inputs.

Why:
- Issue #130806 reports F.embedding crashing on AMD GPUs when the output
  has ~2.1B elements. The root cause is integer overflow in the launch
  configuration computation, not the kernel itself.
- On ROCm, std::min between ceil_div(...) and (mpc*8) cast to ptrdiff_t
  did not behave as expected once outTotalSize exceeded INT_MAX, so the
  block dimension was computed incorrectly. Casting to uint64_t avoids
  the signed overflow, and the largeIndexBlock is now computed directly
  with an explicit ternary ((outTotalSize < 128) ? outTotalSize : 128)
  rather than std::min, sidestepping the ROCm-specific min issue.
- getSliceSize return type updated to size_t to match the unsigned
  arithmetic used by callers and to prevent sign-conversion surprises
  in the grid/block math.

Test:
- Add test_large_tensors in test/nn/test_embedding.py covering the
  reported reproduction (input [131072], weight [16032, 16384],
  output numel 2147483648), guarded by @largeTensorTest("40GB").

Pull Request resolved: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/130806
messages.minimax:
fix: handle large tensor indexing on ROCm by using unsigned types

Change ptrdiff_t to uint64_t/size_t for dimension and size variables in index_add_cuda_impl, index_reduce_func_cuda_impl, and index_select_out_cuda_impl.

The issue had two problems: 1) ptrdiff_t is signed, and outTotalSize of 2147483648 can cause overflow when used in comparisons and arithmetic for kernel launch parameters. 2) On ROCm, std::min -> ::min did not work as expected when values >= 2147483648, causing incorrect block size computation and the "invalid configuration argument" error. Added a test case that reproduces the issue with a 40GB tensor (131072 indices, embedding table 16032x16384, resulting in 2147483648 output elements).

messages.claude:
fix: add missing VSX vector operators for ppc64le build

The VSX (PowerPC) vector implementations were missing explicit
specializations for arithmetic and bitwise operators (+, -, *, /, &,
|, ^) on multiple Vectorized<T> types, including double, float,
int16/int32/int64, qint8/quint8/qint32, and complex float/double.

Why: As reported in issue #128130, PyTorch fails to build on ppc64le
with the error:

  aten/src/ATen/cpu/vec/vec_base.h:632:6: error: use of deleted function
  'double& at::vec::DEFAULT::Vectorized<double>::operator[](int)'

The regression was introduced by commit 457b9f7397c8, which removed
the implicitly-defined operator[] and operator overloads from the
vector base class, expecting each backend (including VSX) to provide
its own explicit specializations. The VSX backend was not updated to
provide these specializations, so generic code paths in
FlashAttentionKernel.cpp (and other native CPU kernels using
`a[i] * b[i]` style indexing) failed to compile because the compiler
fell back to the deleted operator[] instead of vector-level operators.

This change adds the missing operator overloads using the existing
VSX intrinsics (vec_add, vec_sub, vec_mul, vec_div, vec_and, vec_or,
vec_xor) applied per-lane (vec0/vec1), restoring the public operator
surface required by vec_base.h and unblocking the ppc64le build.

Fixes #128130
messages.kimi:
feat: Add missing operator overloads for VSX vectorized types on ppc64le

Add arithmetic (+, -, *, /) and bitwise (&, |, ^) operator overloads for all VSX vectorized types (float, double, complex float, complex double, int16, int32, int64, qint8, quint8, qint32). Also add missing vec0()/vec1() accessor methods to Vectorized<ComplexFlt>.

This fixes the PyTorch build failure on ppc64le (Issue #128130) where the compiler could not find valid operator[] implementations for vectorized operations. The operators are implemented using native VSX intrinsics (vec_add, vec_sub, vec_mul, vec_div, vec_and, vec_or, vec_xor) for optimal performance on POWER architecture.

The C10_ALWAYS_INLINE attribute ensures these operations are properly inlined for maximum performance in tight loops.

This change adds the missing `operator+`, `operator-`, `operator*`, `operator/`, `operator&`, `operator|`, and `operator^` specializations for all VSX-backed Vectorized types (float, double, int32, int64, int16, qint8, qint32, quint8, ComplexFlt, ComplexDbl).

Fixes #128130

Changes to HFStorageWriter to support saving shards of tensors (#154742) (#155566)

Summary:

As we move towards supporting saving partial tensors natively with HFStorageWriter, there are some simple changes that need to be made to make this happen.
- The current approach for distributed writes is that every rank has full tensors, but we split up the writing of these full tensors across all available ranks. We're removing this logic that was in the HFSavePlanner and instead assuming that every rank has a shard and saving every rank's local state
    -  as a result we can probably remove the HFSavePlanner, but keeping it as a placeholder for now

- the current naming of files doesn't support shards as its in the format "model-00001-of-00004.safetensors", but if every rank is writing the same file names they will overwrite eachother, so this adds a shard-00001 prefix, so that the rank files don't overwrite eachother
- don't save the metadata file models.safetensors.index.json if sharding is enabled. This file expects a 1 to 1 ratio between tensor and filename, but this doesn't make sense in the sharded saving approach, so we can just get rid of this file
- make the "fqn_to_file_index" map optional. This is to describe which files to save which tensors in, but if users don't want to provide this, we can just save all the tensors to one file. If they run into issues, they can choose how to split up their tensors to be more friendly with 5GB HF remote storage file size soft limit.

Issue #130658: Internal uses of `torch.load` are missing `weights_only` and raise FutureWarning
### 🐛 Describe the bug

The PyTorch code base contains several uses of `torch.load` internally, but not all of them set `weights_only`, which in PyTorch 2.4 raises a FutureWarning. Since these are internal, the user would see the warning but have no way of acting on it. PyTorch should set `weights_only` in all of its internal uses. 

Some examples (but there are more if you search the code base):
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/f44739cf42e22a569bd1bdb0c113f8a069c17a41/torch/distributed/checkpoint/format_utils.py#L87
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/f44739cf42e22a569bd1bdb0c113f8a069c17a41/torch/distributed/optim/zero_redundancy_optimizer.py#L111

There was a PR recently that resolved one of these important cases:
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/130242

These warnings will show up in PyTorch 2.4. 
This surfaced in our test suite (PyTorch Lightning) since we have configured them to fail if FutureWarning is raised. 

If desired, I can send a PR to fix this.

### Versions

torch=2.4.0

cc @ezyang @gchanan @zou3519 @kadeng @msaroufim @XilunWu @H-Huang @awgu @kwen2501 @wanchaol @fegin @fduwjj @wz337 @wconstab @d4l3k @c-p-i-o @LucasLLC

messages.kimi:
fix: Add `weights_only` parameter to internal `torch.load` calls to suppress FutureWarning

This commit addresses issue #130658 by explicitly setting the `weights_only` parameter in all internal `torch.load` calls within the distributed checkpoint and optimizer modules. 

In PyTorch 2.4, `torch.load` raises a FutureWarning when `weights_only` is not specified. Since these are internal library calls, users would see warnings they cannot act upon. The changes add `weights_only=False` for loading full state dicts (where arbitrary Python objects may be present) and `weights_only=True` for tensor-only loads in the filesystem reader, ensuring consistent behavior and eliminating noise for end users.
messages.minimax:
fix: add explicit weights_only parameter to torch.load calls in DCP

Internal uses of torch.load without weights_only raise FutureWarning in PyTorch 2.4.
This change explicitly sets weights_only=False for checkpoint loading paths where
pickleable objects (optimizers, state dicts) are expected, and weights_only=True
for filesystem reading paths that load tensor-only checkpoints. These are internal
usages so users have no way to suppress the warning otherwise.

Fixes #130658
messages.claude:
fix: set weights_only for internal torch.load calls in DCP

PyTorch 2.4 raises a FutureWarning when torch.load is called without the
weights_only argument, since the default will flip to weights_only=True in
a future release. Several internal call sites in
torch.distributed.checkpoint and torch.distributed.optim did not set this
flag, so end users (e.g. downstream libraries that fail on FutureWarning
like PyTorch Lightning) saw warnings they had no way to act on.

This patch explicitly passes weights_only at every internal call site:
- default_planner.py, format_utils.py, planner.py docs,
  zero_redundancy_optimizer.py: use weights_only=False, since these paths
  load arbitrary pickled objects (e.g. non-tensor state, broadcasted
  objects) that are not pure weight tensors and would fail under the
  restricted unpickler.
- filesystem.py: use weights_only=True, since this path only loads tensor
  storage and can safely use the restricted unpickler.

Resolves #130658.

fix: Handle NaN in CPU Flash Attention when all attention scores are -inf (#127055)

The CPU flash attention kernel produces NaN when all attention scores in a row are -inf (e.g., due to masking). This happens because `exp(-inf - (-inf))` evaluates to `nan`.

Add a check for `tmp_max == -infinity` before computing the exponential. When all scores are -inf, fill the output with zeros instead of proceeding with the softmax computation.

This aligns the CPU flash attention behavior with the math backend, ensuring consistent results when using attention masks that exclude all tokens for certain positions.
messages.claude: pytest test/test_transformers.py -k test_scaled_dot_product_fused_attention_with_inf
messages.minimax:
fix: handle -inf values in CPU FlashAttention kernel to prevent NaN output

Fixes #127055

When all QK values are -inf due to causal/masked attention, computing exp(qk_max - tmp_max) results in exp(-inf - (-inf)) which produces NaN. This change checks for this case and fills the result with zeros instead.

Also adds a regression test that reproduces the bug with a 600x600 mask.

[CUDAGraph Trees] support memory allocation on side stream (#152472)

I tried `beginAllocateToPool` instead of `_cuda_beginAllocateCurrentStreamToPool` and the error in #151199 does not happen any more.

However, this approach is unsafe for multithreading. When multiple run_eager happens concurrently, we expect memory allocation to different mem_pool. Since beginAllocateToPool does not check stream, these memory allocation may happen on the same mem_pool.

So, I use `_cuda_beginAllocateCurrentThreadToPool` to direct all memory allocation on the same thread to a given mem_pool. In particular, `_cuda_beginAllocateCurrentThreadToPool` records the launching thread id, and during runtime checks if the current thread id matches the launching thread id.

Fixes #151199

refactor: Update deprecated `torch.cuda.amp.autocast` to `torch.amp.autocast("cuda", ...)` in parallel_apply.py (#130659)

Replace the deprecated `torch.cuda.amp.autocast` import and usage with the new `torch.amp.autocast("cuda", ...)` API in `torch/nn/parallel/parallel_apply.py`. This eliminates FutureWarnings that users were seeing when using `DataParallel`, which they could not address themselves since the deprecated call was internal to PyTorch.

Fixes #130659
messages.claude:
refactor: replace deprecated `torch.cuda.amp.autocast` with `torch.amp.autocast("cuda", ...)` in parallel_apply

PyTorch 2.4 deprecated `torch.cuda.amp.autocast` in favor of `torch.amp.autocast("cuda", ...)`. However, the internal use in `torch/nn/parallel/parallel_apply.py` was not updated, causing `FutureWarning` to be raised whenever users run `DataParallel` models. Since the warning originates from internal PyTorch code, users have no way to silence it on their end.

This change replaces the deprecated `autocast(enabled=autocast_enabled)` call (imported from `torch.cuda.amp`) with `torch.amp.autocast("cuda", enabled=autocast_enabled)`, and removes the now-unused import. This aligns the internal codebase with the public API guidance and eliminates spurious warnings for DP users.

Refs: #130659

messages.kimi:
fix: [MPS] Fix batch norm incorrect results with sliced inputs

Fixes #133520

The MPS batch norm implementation was incorrectly handling non-contiguous tensors (such as tensor slices) by unconditionally applying a gather operation. When the input tensor was already in the expected memory format, the gather operation was unnecessary and could produce incorrect results.

Remove the `executeGatherOp` logic that was incorrectly determining when to apply the gather operation. The `Placeholder` class already handles the necessary stride checks internally, making this manual check redundant and error-prone.

Add regression test `test_batch_norm_slices` to verify batch norm produces correct results when operating on sliced tensors.
messages.claude:
fix: [MPS] Fix batch norm with sliced inputs

Fixes #133520

The batch norm MPS kernel incorrectly assumed that contiguous inputs (in
the requested memory format) could skip the gather op used to materialize
a dense copy before running the MPS graph. When the input is a
non-trivial slice (e.g. `x[5:]`), `self.is_contiguous(memory_format)`
returns true for the sliced view even though the underlying storage
offset and strides do not match what the cached graph expects, producing
incorrect numerical results. This manifested as FLUX.1-schnell producing
inconsistent outputs on MPS (regression introduced during the 2.3.x ->
nightly window per bisect in the issue).

Drop the `executeGatherOp` short-circuit and always pass the input
through `Placeholder` with the gather path enabled, so sliced and
non-contiguous inputs are materialized into a dense tensor that matches
the cached graph's placeholder shape.

Add `test_batch_norm_slices` regression test comparing MPS and CPU
BatchNorm2d outputs on a sliced input (`x[5:]`).

Pull Request resolved: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/133521
Approved by: https://github.com/malfet

messages.kimi:
fix: Fix workspace allocation with symbolic nbytes in cpp_wrapper_cuda

The issue #131337 reports an AssertionError when running test_consecutive_split_cumprod_cuda with TORCHINDUCTOR_ABI_COMPATIBLE=1 and TORCHINDUCTOR_CPP_WRAPPER=1. The root cause is that generate_workspace_allocation receives a sympy.Expr for nbytes instead of a concrete integer, causing a mismatch in call_args and arg_types.

This fix:
1. In wrapper.py: Convert sympy.Expr nbytes to a concrete size hint using V.graph.sizevars.size_hint() before allocation
2. In cpp_wrapper_cuda.py: Handle symbolic nbytes by using the default workspace.zero_() behavior instead of aoti_torch_zero_(), since the AOTI service platform doesn't have the zero_() symbol for dynamic shapes

The test skip for test_consecutive_split_cumprod_cuda_dynamic_shapes is removed as the test now passes.
messages.minimax:
fix: handle symbolic nbytes in workspace allocation for cpp wrapper

When nbytes is a symbolic expression (sympy.Expr), the cpp wrapper codegen was failing with "call_args and arg_types do not match" because it couldn't properly handle dynamic sizes. This change adds a size_hint conversion for symbolic nbytes in the base wrapper and uses the simpler zero_() call directly when nbytes is symbolic, avoiding the aoti_torch_zero_ wrapper that expects concrete types. The test skip for test_consecutive_split_cumprod_cuda_dynamic_shapes is removed as the underlying issue is now fixed.
messages.claude:
[cpp_wrapper] Fix workspace allocation for dynamic shapes

Fixes #131337

When the workspace allocation size is a symbolic expression (sympy.Expr),
the C++ wrapper previously emitted code referencing the symbolic nbytes
directly into the generated C++ source. This caused a mismatch between
the number of call_args and arg_types at codegen time, surfacing as
`AssertionError: call_args and arg_types do not match` in
`generate_kernel_call` for dynamic-shape tests such as
`test_consecutive_split_cumprod_cuda_dynamic_shapes`.

The root cause is twofold:
1. In `wrapper.py`, `generate_workspace_allocation` did not resolve the
   symbolic nbytes into a concrete integer before building the
   allocation call, so the emitted call signature did not line up with
   the recorded argument types.
2. In `cpp_wrapper_cuda.py`, the `zero_()` path branched unconditionally
   on the AOTI `aoti_torch_zero_` symbol, which the service platform does
   not yet expose. Mixing this with a symbolic nbytes broke codegen for

context.issue:
Issue #133415: Init Optim State in Checkpointing Does not Apply to Stateless Optimizers
### 🐛 Describe the bug

The new API for checkpointing, e.g. `set_optimizer_state_dict`, calls `_init_optim_state`.

https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/2a4304329be0ee592af0f1d8d0dd9428ed82a0c6/torch/distributed/checkpoint/state_dict.py#L585-L605

This function will initialize optimizer states if they are not already initialized by doing a step with grads as zero. 

However, this causes problems for stateless optimizers, e.g. SGD. For example, if I have a simple code snippet where I train a model, save it, and then load it, using the standard training loop structure:
```
for i, data in enumerate(train_loader, 0):
    # Get the inputs; data is a tuple of (inputs, labels)
    inputs, labels = data

    # Zero the parameter gradients
    optimizer.zero_grad()

    # Forward pass
    outputs = model(inputs)
    loss = loss_function(outputs, labels)

    # Backward pass and optimize
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()

    # Periodically checkpoint
    
# Load checkpoint   
 
# Resume training from ckpt
for i, data in enumerate(train_loader, 0):  
    # Get the inputs; data is a tuple of (inputs, labels)
    inputs, labels = data

    # Zero the parameter gradients
    optimizer.zero_grad()

    # Forward pass
    outputs = model(inputs)
    loss = loss_function(outputs, labels)

    # Backward pass and optimize
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()

    # Periodically checkpoint

```
this will fail as `optimizer.zero_grad()` is typically called before the forward pass. Accordingly, the resume from checkpoint call will fail for SGD as it will call `_init_optim_states`, which will raise an error. This is because state is not set (as SGD has no state) but grads are non-zero in the standard training loop set up.

Instead, I believe that the init call should check if the optimizer is a stateless optimizer. 

### Versions

PyTorch 2.4

cc @XilunWu @H-Huang @awgu @kwen2501 @wanchaol @fegin @fduwjj @wz337 @wconstab @d4l3k @c-p-i-o

messages.minimax:
fix: handle stateless optimizers in _init_optim_state for checkpoint state dict

The _init_optim_state function was raising an error when gradients exist but the optimizer is stateless (e.g., SGD). For stateless optimizers, the state is not initialized through step() calls, so they never have optimizer state to initialize. Instead of erroring, the function should return early if gradients are already present, as this indicates the model has already been used in training and no state initialization is needed. Also added torch.optim.SGD to the test matrix and adjusted learning rates to 1e-4 for consistency.
messages.claude:
fix: support stateless optimizers in checkpointing _init_optim_state

The previous implementation of `_init_optim_state` raised a RuntimeError
when gradients were non-None but optimizer state was uninitialized. This
broke checkpointing for stateless optimizers like SGD, where
`zero_grad()` is typically called before the forward pass in a standard
training loop. After `zero_grad()`, grads can still be non-None (set to
zero), so resuming from a checkpoint would incorrectly raise an error
even though SGD has no state to initialize.

This change updates the logic to return early when any parameter has a
non-None gradient, since the optimizer is either stateful with already
initialized state or stateless (like SGD) and needs no initialization.
When gradients are None, the existing zero-gradient initialization is
safe because stateless optimizers like SGD will no-op with zero grads
and zero lr. A comment is added to explain this reasoning.

Test coverage is extended to include `torch.optim.SGD` across the FSDP,
DDP, and related state_dict tests so the checkpoint path is exercised
for stateless optimizers. The learning rate is lowered from 1e-3 to 1e-4
to keep training stable enough for value comparisons, and the test
training loop is restructured to zero grads before the forward/backward
pass for both the original and distributed optimizers, matching the
training loop pattern described in the issue. A small improvement to
`_verify_msd` surfaces the mismatched FQN and tensor values on assertion
failure to aid debugging.
messages.kimi:
Looking at the code changes and the issue, I need to understand what's happening:

1. The Issue (#133415): The `_init_optim_state` function in `torch/distributed/checkpoint/state_dict.py` fails for stateless optimizers like SGD. When loading a checkpoint, if gradients exist (from the standard training loop where `zero_grad()` is called before forward), the function raises a RuntimeError because it expects either initialized optimizer states or None gradients.

2. The Fix: The code change modifies `_init_optim_state` to:
   - Return early if the optimizer is stateless (no state to initialize)
   - Allow the function to proceed when gradients exist (instead of raising an error)
   - The comment explains: "There are some stateless optimizers like SGD. These optimizer will not return in the above condition. So if gradients exist, we should also return."

3. Test Changes: The tests are updated to:
   - Include SGD in the optimizer classes being tested
   - Fix the training loop order (zero_grad before forward, step after backward)
   - Reduce learning rate from 1e-3 to 1e-4 for numerical stability
   - Add better error messages for tensor comparison failures

4. Commit Type: This is a fix - it's fixing a bug where stateless optimizers (SGD) couldn't be used with checkpointing.

Based on the reference examples, I'll write a commit message that follows the pattern:

test(distributed/checkpoint): fix state dict initialization for stateless optimizers

Fix the `_init_optim_state` function to properly handle stateless optimizers like SGD. Previously, the function would raise a RuntimeError when gradients existed but optimizer states weren't initialized, which broke the standard training loop pattern where `zero_grad()` is called before the forward pass. The fix allows early return when gradients exist, since stateless optimizers don't need state initialization. Also update tests to include SGD and fix the training loop order to match standard practice (zero_grad before forward, step after backward). Reduce learning rate from 1e-3 to 1e-4 for numerical stability.

Fixes #133415

context.issue:
Issue #131701: `/opt/rocm/lib/libamdhip64.so` is hardcoded in `Caffe2Targets.cmake` in ROCm wheels
### 🐛 Describe the bug

`/opt/rocm` is hardcoded in `Caffe2Targets.cmake` in ROCm wheels:

```sh
wget https://download.pytorch.org/whl/rocm6.1/torch-2.4.0%2Brocm6.1-cp312-cp312-linux_x86_64.whl
unzip torch-2.4.0+rocm6.1-cp312-cp312-linux_x86_64.whl
cd torch/share/cmake/Caffe2
```

You can find below in `Caffe2Targets.cmake`:

```cmake
set_target_properties(c10_hip PROPERTIES
  INTERFACE_INCLUDE_DIRECTORIES "${_IMPORT_PREFIX}/include"
  INTERFACE_LINK_LIBRARIES "c10;/opt/rocm/lib/libamdhip64.so"                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 
)
```

```cmake
set_target_properties(torch_hip PROPERTIES
  INTERFACE_COMPILE_DEFINITIONS "USE_C10D_NCCL"
  INTERFACE_COMPILE_OPTIONS "-fPIC;-D__HIP_PLATFORM_AMD__=1;-DCUDA_HAS_FP16=1;-DUSE_ROCM;-D__HIP_NO_HALF_OPERATORS__=1;-D__HIP_NO_HALF_CONVERSIONS__=1;-DTORCH_HIP_VERSION=601;-Wno-shift-count-negative;-Wno-shift-count-overflow;-Wno-duplicate-decl-specifier;-DCAFFE2_USE_MIOPEN;-DTHRUST_DEVICE_SYSTEM=THRUST_DEVICE_SYSTEM_HIP;-std=c++17;-DHIPBLAS_V2;-DHIP_NEW_TYPE_ENUMS"
  INTERFACE_INCLUDE_DIRECTORIES "${_IMPORT_PREFIX}/include"
  INTERFACE_LINK_LIBRARIES "c10_hip;torch_cpu_library;/opt/rocm/lib/libamdhip64.so;MIOpen;/opt/rocm/lib/libhiprtc.so;/opt/rocm/lib/libroctx64.so;roc::hipblaslt;roc::hipblas;hip::hipfft;hip::hiprand;roc::hipsparse;roc::hipsolver"
)
```

In some HPCs, the ROCm may not be installed in `/opt/rocm`, but in other directories such as `/opt/rocm-6.0.0`. When a third-party package uses `find_package(Torch)` and links with PyTorch libraries (which is suggested by [the tutorial](https://pytorch.org/tutorials/advanced/torch_script_custom_ops.html#building-with-cmake)), it may introduce an invalid link library.

@Slaedr originally posted this problem in https://github.com/deepmodeling/deepmd-kit/issues/4008 (our package that links with PyTorch libraries).

I noticed there was a similar issue in other PyTorch modules https://github.com/pytorch/kineto/issues/838.

### Versions

Not related to the runtime environment

cc @ezyang @gchanan @zou3519 @kadeng @msaroufim @jeffdaily @sunway513 @jithunnair-amd @pruthvistony @ROCmSupport @dllehr-amd @jataylo @hongxiayang

messages.claude:
build: replace hardcoded ROCm lib paths with imported CMake targets

Replace raw library references (e.g. `${PYTORCH_HIP_LIBRARIES}` resolving to
`/opt/rocm/lib/libamdhip64.so`) with CMake imported targets (`hip::amdhip64`,
`MIOpen`, `hiprtc::hiprtc`, `roc::hipblaslt`) in c10/hip and Caffe2 HIP
dependency lists. Also add `hiprtc` to find_package calls in LoadHIP.cmake so
the imported target is available.

Why: the previous configuration baked the absolute `/opt/rocm/lib/...` path
into the generated `Caffe2Targets.cmake` shipped inside ROCm wheels. On HPC
systems where ROCm is installed under a non-standard prefix (e.g.
`/opt/rocm-6.0.0`), downstream projects calling `find_package(Torch)` ended up
with invalid link libraries pointing at a non-existent `/opt/rocm` location
(issue #131701). Using CMake's imported targets lets the consumer's ROCm
installation be resolved at config time via `find_dependency`, eliminating the
hardcoded path and making PyTorch linkable against ROCm installs in arbitrary
locations.

Pull Request resolved: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/131701

This ensures that ROCm library paths are resolved at configure time rather than being hardcoded to /opt/rocm/lib in the installed Caffe2Targets.cmake, which caused linking failures on systems with ROCm installed in non-standard locations.

feat: enable AOTriton flash attention support for Navi31 GPUs and fix CUDA Graph RNG handling

Bump AOTriton to 0.7b (switching release artifact from .tar.bz2 to .tar.gz) and wire up the new seed/offset tensor-based RNG API so dropout states flow correctly under CUDA graph capture.

What:
- Bump AOTriton pin to 0.7b and update install script to use .tar.gz tarball
- Add experimental flash/mem-efficient attention support for gfx1100 (Navi31), gated behind TORCH_ROCM_AOTRITON_ENABLE_EXPERIMENTAL env var
- Adapt attn_fwd/attn_bwd calls to the new AOTriton API that accepts TensorView-based seed/offset (with philox_state path for capture streams) instead of raw int64 values
- Place seed_t/offset_t on CUDA for the ROCm path; add mk_aoscalartensor / mk_philoxtensor adapters
- Disable GQA on ROCm (backend_supports_grouped_query_attention=false) since AOTriton does not yet support it
- Adjust SDPA test tolerances and skip conditions for ROCm (causal+fp32, GQA, is_causal with unequal seq_len)

Why:
- Issue #133540 reports test_scaled_dot_product_attention_cuda failing on ROCm main. The AOTriton 0.7b bump and API migration bring the kernel calls in sync with upstream, and the CUDA-graph-safe philox_state path fixes dropout RNG capture that previously broke under graph capture.

- GQA is disabled on ROCm because the AOTriton flash backend does not yet implement grouped-query attention; the test skip and sample-input changes prevent false failures rather than masking real bugs.
- Test fudge factors and skips are tuned for ROCm's numerical behavior so the gradient checks fail on real regressions instead of platform noise (e.g. causal+fp32 large errors, longer-sequence grad divergence).

Extend the assertion node removal pass to handle additional zero-output
ATen operations including _assert_async.default, _assert_scalar.default,

messages.claude:
[ONNX] Handle zero-output aten assertion ops in FX pass

The `remove_assertion_nodes` FX pass previously only stripped
`aten._assert_async.msg` and `aten.sym_constrain_range_for_size.default`
from the graph. When the exporter encountered other assertion variants
emitted by torch.export — namely `aten._assert_async.default`,
`aten._assert_scalar.default`, and `aten._assert_tensor_metadata.default` —
those nodes were left in the graph, breaking ONNX export for models that
contain them (e.g. models with shape guards or runtime assertions).

These ops produce zero outputs and carry no semantic meaning for the
exported ONNX graph, so they should be removed alongside the already-
handled assertion targets. Adding them to the target set ensures the
pass cleans up all assertion variants consistently.

Adds a regression test that exports a model containing
`aten._assert_async.msg` to guard against future regressions.

Fixes #135419

Looking at the code change and the related issue, I can see this is a fix for the XPU wheel build configuration.

Summary (What): Skip adding triton dependency for XPU wheel builds

Reason (Why): The issue #143838 reports that PyTorch XPU 2.6 RC wheels have multiple triton dependencies (both `triton` and `pytorch-triton-xpu`). The fix adds a condition to exclude XPU builds from the triton dependency injection, preventing duplicate/conflicting triton packages in XPU wheels.

The change modifies `.circleci/scripts/binary_populate_env.sh` to check if `PYTORCH_BUILD_VERSION` contains "xpu" and skip the triton requirement addition for XPU builds.

fix: Skip triton dependency for XPU wheel builds

XPU wheels were incorrectly including both `triton` and `pytorch-triton-xpu` dependencies, causing conflicts during installation. This change adds a version check to exclude XPU builds from the generic triton dependency injection, ensuring XPU wheels only depend on `pytorch-triton-xpu`. Fixes #143838.

Issue #140318: Visible devices are not respected on AMD systems
### 🐛 Describe the bug

When running distributed (or multi-process) jobs on AMD GPU systems with GPU isolation (i.e., the `*_VISIBLE_DEVICES` environment variable), PyTorch still tries to set the seed of all the devices it finds. This causes the following exception to be raised:

```
File "/path/to/torch/random.py", line 46, in manual_seed                                                                                               
  torch.cuda.manual_seed_all(seed)                                                                                                                                                                      
File "/path/to/torch/cuda/random.py", line 131, in manual_seed_all                                                                                    
  _lazy_call(cb, seed_all=True)                                                                                                                                                                        
File "/path/to/torch/cuda/__init__.py", line 249, in _lazy_call                                                                                       
  callable()                                                                                                                                                                                            
File "/path/to/torch/cuda/random.py", line 128, in cb                                                                                                  
  default_generator = torch.cuda.default_generators[i]                                                                                                                                                 
                      ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~^^^                                                                                                                                                 
IndexError: tuple index out of range
```


The underlying issue is that the visible devices are not properly detected due to reading the wrong environment variable name: `HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES` should be renamed to `ROCR_VISIBLE_DEVICES` (see https://rocm.docs.amd.com/en/latest/conceptual/gpu-isolation.html#rocr-visible-devices ). On many batch schedulers and clusters, the ROCr environment variable is the one that is set.

This was likely introduced in #119182 (cc @jeffdaily @sunway513 @jithunnair-amd @pruthvistony @ROCmSupport @dllehr-amd @jataylo @hongxiayang @naromero77amd)

I

messages.kimi:
feat: Add support for ROCR_VISIBLE_DEVICES on AMD systems

Add support for the ROCR_VISIBLE_DEVICES environment variable alongside HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES when parsing visible devices on AMD GPU systems. ROCR_VISIBLE_DEVICES is processed first as it filters the GPUs available to HIP, and when both are set, HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES is preferred but validated against ROCR's device count. This fixes the IndexError that occurred when PyTorch tried to access GPUs that were hidden by ROCR_VISIBLE_DEVICES but not recognized by the existing HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES check.
messages.minimax:
fix(cuda): respect ROCR_VISIBLE_DEVICES on AMD HIP systems

On AMD GPU systems, batch schedulers and cluster environments set
ROCR_VISIBLE_DEVICES rather than HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES to isolate GPUs.
This caused IndexError when running distributed/multi-process jobs because
the visible devices were not properly detected (issue #140318).

Now checks ROCR_VISIBLE_DEVICES first and uses it to determine device
count. HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES takes precedence if both are set, with a
sanity check to ensure it doesn't exceed the ROCR device count.
messages.claude:
fix: Respect ROCR_VISIBLE_DEVICES on AMD GPU systems

Summary: On AMD/ROCm systems, PyTorch only honored HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES and ignored ROCR_VISIBLE_DEVICES, which is the environment variable that ROCr (and many batch schedulers/clusters) actually set for GPU isolation. As a result, the visible device set was mis-parsed, the device count was wrong, and downstream code (e.g. torch.cuda.manual_seed_all) raised IndexError when indexing default_generators beyond the visible range.

Why: Issue #140318 reports that visible devices are not respected on AMD systems, causing distributed/multi-process jobs to crash with `IndexError: tuple index out of range` in manual_seed_all. Per ROCm's GPU isolation model, ROCR_VISIBLE_DEVICES is processed first by the runtime and reduces the pool of GPUs that HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES can subsequently select from. Parsing HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES alone therefore yields an incorrect device list whenever only ROCR_VISIBLE_DEVICES is set (the common case on real clusters).

This change extends _parse_visible_devices() to read ROCR_VISIBLE_DEVICES alongside HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES:
- When only ROCR_VISIBLE_DEVICES is set, the visible devices are derived as list(range(rocr_count)) since ROCR has already filtered the device pool and the HIP-visible indices are the leading N devices.
- When both env vars are set, HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES is preferred (it selects a subset of the ROCR-filtered pool), with a sanity check that raises RuntimeError if HIP claims more devices than ROCR exposes, since that configuration is contradictory.
- When only HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES is set, behavior is unchanged.

Tests in test/test_cuda.py::test_hip_device_count cover the two new ROCR/HIP combinations.

pr_title: Fix batch-specific attention mod for NJT + Flex

exemplars.message:
[Inductor][FlexAttention] fix `vars_and_sizes` divisor error (#151634)

Triton codegen currently [sorts vars by divisor](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/ae6f6b8efb6380a94621d61100ffb05dab05db27/torch/_inductor/codegen/simd.py#L233-L237). When there are two vars with the same divisor, the order is undecided.

```python
nodes.sort(
   key=lambda x: V.graph.sizevars.size_hint(
       x.divisor, fallback=config.unbacked_symint_fallback
   )
)
```

The test case leads to the following nodes:
```
(Pdb) nodes[0]
IterationRangesEntry(x1, ((s37 + 127)//128), 2, (xindex//ps0), {x0: ((s37 + 127)//128), x1: 2, x2: ((s12 + 127)//128), x4: 2*(((s12 + 127)//128))*(((s37 + 127)//128)), x5: 0, x6: 2, x7: (((s12 + 127)//128))*(((s37 + 127)//128))})

(Pdb) nodes[1]
IterationRangesEntry(x0, 1, ((s37 + 127)//128), ModularIndexing(xindex, 1, ps0), {x0: ((s37 + 127)//128), x1: 2, x2: ((s12 + 127)//128), x4: 2*(((s12 + 127)//128))*(((s37 + 127)//128)), x5: 0, x6: 2, x7: (((s12 + 127)//128))*(((s37 + 127)//128))})

(Pdb) nodes[2]
IterationRangesEntry(x2, 2*(((s37 + 127)//128)), ((s12 + 127)//128), (xindex//(2*(((s37 + 127)//128)))), {x0: ((s37 + 127)//128), x1: 2, x2: ((s12 + 127)//128), x4: 2*(((s12 + 127)//128))*(((s37 + 127)//128)), x5: 0, x6: 2, x7: (((s12 + 127)//128))*(((s37 + 127)//128))})

(Pdb) V.graph.sizevars.statically_known_equals(nodes[0].length, 2)
True
(Pdb) V.graph.sizevars.statically_known_equals(nodes[1].length, 1)
True
(Pdb) V.graph.sizevars.statically_known_equals(nodes[2].length, 1)
True

(Pdb) V.graph.sizevars.statically_known_equals(nodes[0].divisor, 1)
True
(Pdb) V.graph.sizevars.statically_known_equals(nodes[1].divisor, 1)
True
(Pdb) V.graph.sizevars.statically_known_equals(nodes[2].divisor, 2)
True
```

Since x1 and x0 both have divisor 1, the relative order is random across runs.
In some runs, we have order [x1, x0, x2] with divisors as [1,1,2] and lengths as [2,1,1]. After x1, we have [divisor = divisor * node.length](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/ae6f6b8efb6380a94621d61100ffb05dab05db27/torch/_inductor/codegen/simd.py#L246) = 1 * 2 = 2. Then, when processing x0, we have node.divisor=1, divisor=2, and [FloorDiv(node.divisor, divisor)](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/ae6f6b8efb6380a94621d61100ffb05dab05db27/torch/_inductor/codegen/simd.py#L251) = 0, which indicates an iteration length of 0 and leads errors later.

The fix is to sort by both divisor and length_is_one. So for two nodes with the same divisor, we process the node with length=1 first.

Issue #143788: Flex attention with nested tensors, bug in `create_nested_block_mask`
The following code is from `_nested_mod_func_adapter` which is a helper function used by `create_nested_block_mask`. Conceptually, it wraps a mod function that operates on individual batch items of a nested tensor and transforms the inputs so it works on a single packed item. However, the below code doesn't appear to update the batch argument (`b`) before calling the original mod function.

https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/6ccb8ed1868984d9d2ea4e48a085508d1027cd9b/torch/nn/attention/flex_attention.py#L985-L990

Since `create_nested_block_mask` effectively packs all the batch items from the nested tensor into a single item, it appears like the helper should do something like `b_nested = q_seq_idx[q_idx]` and pass that in place of `b` to `orig_mod_func`.

Otherwise, it appears that the wrapped mod func has no way of knowing which batch item it's operating on.
